beats.beat: Owen asks Rowe plainly what his intentions are, since his sister's name is now in every kitchen in Amberlight.
Rowe, startled into honesty, admits he does not know what to call his feeling, only that it is slower and better than the gossip allows.
Word arrives that Louisa's uncle has agreed to fit the old east wing of Amberlight House as a schoolroom at the estate's expense, needing no subscription at all.
Rowe realizes that with the money settled, he has no more useful reason to marry, only whatever reason is left over, which is Judith herself.
He sets out to find her and meets her already on the road to his lodging, come to settle the matter of the gossip herself.

turn.note: Judith's arrival to settle the matter herself, rather than let it be settled between the two men, redirects chapter 7 toward her taking the lead.

problems: One coordinated clause chain changes shape: 'He will not sell, and he will not pull anything down, and he has agreed to have the old east wing at the house fitted for a school at the estate's charge' shifts from two negatives to a positive third clause; split after 'pull anything down.'

generic_prose.quote: with the look of a woman who has spent an hour deciding something and does not mean to be talked out of it in the road

trope_note: Enemies of manner resolves honestly through Rowe's confession, and the chaperone's-absence fallout drives Owen's confrontation; Mrs Pike's matchmaking is absent this chapter but was already inverted last chapter, so no beat is owed her here.
fixes: Split 'He will not sell, and he will not pull anything down, and he has agreed to have the old east wing at the house fitted for a school at the estate's charge' after the second clause; the third clause changes shape and should start its own sentence.

The chapter runs well over its 560-word target (roughly 620). Trim the recap paragraph 'He had carried the figure into Hollis's yard and Mrs Yardley's parlour and up to Mrs Pike's table in a brushed coat and a new neckcloth...' — it restates facts from chapters 1 and 3 and can be cut to a single clause.
Replace 'Owen looked at him for a while' with a concrete beat of action rather than a flat narrated pause.
Give Judith's approach a physical detail in place of 'the look of a woman who has spent an hour deciding something' so the moment is seen rather than summarized.

writer_note:
This story is now read by a single narrator rather than a
cast with a voice each, so the prose has to carry who is speaking. It was
written under the old rule, which forbade attribution because the voices made it
redundant.

Go through the chapter and add attribution wherever a listener — who cannot see
the page, and cannot look back — would lose track of who is speaking. A tag
belongs in its own narrator segment: `said Mrs Pike`, `Rowe said`, or an action
that does the same work: *Rowe turned the note over.* Two people alternating in
a plain exchange do not need one every line; the third turn usually does, and so
does every return to dialogue after narration, and every line in a scene of
three or more.

Do not attribute every line. An unbroken column of `said X` is padding, and it
is the opposite failure.

Where a line would be misread without it, you may add a `tag` to that segment —
`"[quietly]"`, `"[a beat]"`, `"[warmly]"` — as performance direction for the
voice. It is never printed and never spoken. A few a chapter at most, and never
to imitate a different person: one voice reads everyone.

Come back no longer than you started. These chapters are already at or over
their word ceiling, and attribution adds words — so take them back out of
restatement: a line of dialogue that lands followed by narration explaining that
it landed, a room established twice. If you come back long the check sends the
chapter straight back to be cut, which spends a revision on arithmetic instead
of on the prose.

Change nothing else. Same events, same beats, same jokes, same last line.
